lessons.title: Leverage in Action: How Debt Magnifies Returns and Risks

children.text: Leverage is the most seductive idea in corporate finance. Borrow at 10%, deploy at 20%, and the difference belongs entirely to the shareholders. It works exactly as promised, which is the problem: the same mechanism runs in reverse with equal force, and nothing warns you when the direction is about to change.
This lesson runs one company through nine combinations of leverage and performance so you can see both directions in the same table.

body.text: Leverage does not create returns. It magnifies whatever the business already produces, upwards when the business earns more than the debt costs, downwards when it earns less.

children.text: Two Different Returns
Two ratios matter here, and confusing them is the root of most bad leverage decisions.
[[Return on capital employed]]
measures the business itself: operating profit against all the capital in it, borrowed and owned. It has nothing to do with how the company is funded.
[[Return on equity]]
measures the shareholders' outcome, after interest and tax. It depends heavily on how the company is funded.
Leverage is the bridge between them, and the direction it pushes depends on a single comparison.

body.caption: The middle term is leverage. It is positive only when ROCE exceeds the cost of debt

body.text: Read the bracket. If ROCE is above the cost of debt, the term adds to ROE and grows with the debt-to-equity ratio. If ROCE falls below it, the same term subtracts, and grows just as fast. Leverage has no opinion about which way it works.

children.text: One Company, Nine Outcomes
Take a company with ₹100 crore of capital employed, borrowing at 10% before tax, paying tax at an effective 25.17%. Run it at three leverage levels and three levels of business performance.

stats.label: Swing caused by leverage
stats.context: Same business, same assets, different funding

body.title: The upside case
body.prompt: Using the table above, what is the return on equity in a strong year with ₹75 crore of debt, in percent? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: EBIT of ₹20 crore less ₹7.5 crore of interest leaves ₹12.5 crore. After tax at 25.17% that is about ₹9.35 crore, earned on just ₹25 crore of equity, which is 37.4%. The unlevered company earned 14.97% on the same assets. Leverage did not improve the business at all.

body.title: The downside case
body.prompt: Same company, weak year with ROCE of 6% and ₹75 crore of debt. EBIT is ₹6 crore and interest is ₹7.5 crore. What is the return on equity, in percent? Use a negative number for a loss.
body.explanation: Interest of ₹7.5 crore exceeds EBIT of ₹6 crore, so the company loses ₹1.5 crore before tax and there is no tax shield to soften it. On ₹25 crore of equity that is minus 6%. The unlevered company still earned a positive 4.49% in the same conditions.

children.text: The Break-Even Nobody Calculates
There is one level of business performance at which leverage does nothing at all. It is when ROCE exactly equals the cost of debt.

body.caption: The neutral point: ROCE of 10%, cost of debt 10%

children.text: Identical returns, wildly different risk. The company on the right has committed to ₹7.5 crore of annual interest for exactly no gain. This is the position a great many businesses are actually in, because they borrowed on the strength of a good year and now run at a return close to their borrowing cost.

body.title: The single test
body.textWithBlank: Leverage improves returns for shareholders only when the return on capital employed is higher than the ___ of debt.
body.explanation: Above the cost of debt, borrowing adds to the owners' return. Below it, borrowing subtracts. At exactly that level it adds risk and nothing else.

body.text: Notice what decides the outcome. It is not the interest rate on its own, and not the debt level on its own. It is the gap between what the business earns on capital and what the debt costs. A company with a thin, volatile ROCE is dangerous at leverage a utility would find conservative.

children.text: Why the Downside Is Worse Than the Table Suggests
The nine-outcome table understates the danger, because it assumes only one thing changes. In a real downturn, several move at once.
Interest does not fall with profits.
It is the one cost that ignores your revenue entirely.
Covenants break.
As Lesson 3.3 showed, the ratios fail because profit dropped, handing the lender new rights at the worst moment.
Refinancing gets harder and dearer.
A weak year raises your spread just as you need to roll over debt.
Working capital tightens.
Suppliers shorten credit to a company that looks stretched, which consumes cash exactly when there is less of it.
Management attention shifts.
Senior people spend their weeks on lender meetings rather than on customers.

body.title: Financial leverage and operating leverage compound each other

children.text: financial leverage
comes from fixed interest.
operating leverage
comes from fixed operating costs: rent, salaries, plant. Both magnify the effect of a change in revenue, and a business carrying a lot of each is far more fragile than either one alone suggests.

markDefs.definition: The use of borrowed money to increase the return earned on the owners' capital, and the losses too.
The effect of fixed operating costs. A business with high fixed costs sees profits swing more sharply when revenue moves.

children.text: A hotel, an airline, a steel plant or a cinema chain has high operating leverage: most costs continue whether or not customers arrive.
A services firm or a distribution business has low operating leverage: costs fall roughly with activity.
Adding heavy debt to a high operating leverage business stacks one multiplier on another. That combination is behind a large share of Indian corporate distress.

The practical rule: the more fixed your operating costs, the less fixed your financing costs should be. Businesses with volatile revenue belong at the low-leverage end regardless of how cheap debt looks.

body.label: What a decade of leveraged expansion produced
body.value: The RBI's 2017 list of 12 large stressed accounts
body.context: After the infrastructure and commodities boom of roughly 2007 to 2012, several Indian groups had borrowed heavily against projects whose returns arrived late or never. In 2017 the RBI directed banks to refer twelve of the largest defaulting accounts, including Essar Steel, Bhushan Steel and Lanco Infratech, to insolvency proceedings. Those companies did not fail because interest rates rose. They failed because the return on the capital they had deployed fell below the cost of the debt funding it, and stayed there.

children.text: The Other Way to a High ROE
Leverage is one route to a high return on equity. It is not the only one, and it is the fragile one.

body.title: Two ways a company reaches a 25% return on equity

columns.label: Through leverage
points: Modest ROCE, amplified by a high debt-to-equity ratio
Reverses violently in a weak year
Constrained by covenants and lender confidence

columns.label: Through the business
points: High ROCE from pricing power, capital efficiency or scale
Survives weak years with lower but positive returns
Indian IT services firms are the standard example: high ROE, almost no borrowing

body.text: When you see a high ROE on screener.in, always check the debt-to-equity ratio next to it. Two companies showing 25% can be completely different animals: one is a strong business, the other is an average business with a large loan. The second will not look the same in a downturn.

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Open any listed company and compare ROCE against ROE, then look at debt to equity. When ROE is far above ROCE, leverage is doing the work. When they are close, the business is.

body.title: Diagnose the ROE
body.question: Company X reports ROCE of 11% and ROE of 26%. Company Y reports ROCE of 27% and ROE of 25%. Both operate in the same industry. What does this tell you?
options: Company X is the better business, because its ROE is higher
Company X is using substantial leverage to lift a modest business return, while Company Y earns its return from operations
body.explanation: When ROE sits far above ROCE, borrowed money is doing the work. When the two are close, the business is. Company X's 26% depends on the gap between its 11% ROCE and its cost of debt holding up. If ROCE slips to 8%, that 26% collapses, while Company Y would still be earning well.

body.title: When does more debt hurt?
body.question: A company earns ROCE of 9% and can borrow at 11%. It doubles its debt to fund more of the same business. What happens to return on equity?
options: It rises, because debt is cheaper than equity
It falls, because each additional rupee borrowed earns 9% and costs 11%
It rises only if the tax shield is counted
body.explanation: Every rupee borrowed loses 2 percentage points before tax. Leverage multiplies a negative gap just as efficiently as a positive one, so ROE falls and keeps falling as debt rises. The tax shield reduces the cost of debt but does not close a 2 point gap.

body.title: Two competitors, one bad year
body.scenario: Nandan Ceramics and Prakash Tiles are fictional competitors in Morbi, each with ₹200 crore of capital employed and near-identical operations. Nandan funds itself with ₹40 crore of debt at 10% and ₹160 crore of equity. Prakash funds itself with ₹140 crore of debt at 10.5% and ₹60 crore of equity. In a normal year both earn ROCE of 16%. Then a gas price spike and a weak export market cut ROCE to 5% for two consecutive years. Tax is 25.17%, and both have covenants requiring interest cover above 2x.
body.prompt: Work out what happens to each company, and what it means for how they emerge from the downturn.
body.modelAnswer:
Normal year:
Nandan: EBIT ₹32 crore, interest ₹4 crore, PBT ₹28 crore, PAT about ₹20.95 crore on ₹160 crore of equity, so ROE of about 13.1%. Interest cover 8x.
Prakash: EBIT ₹32 crore, interest ₹14.7 crore, PBT ₹17.3 crore, PAT about ₹12.95 crore on ₹60 crore of equity, so ROE of about 21.6%. Interest cover about 2.2x. Prakash looks like the better-run company, and in a good year its shareholders do better.

Downturn, ROCE 5%:
Nandan: EBIT ₹10 crore, interest ₹4 crore, PBT ₹6 crore, PAT about ₹4.49 crore, ROE about 2.8%. Interest cover 2.5x, so the covenant holds. Painful but survivable.
Prakash: EBIT ₹10 crore, interest ₹14.7 crore, so a pre-tax loss of ₹4.7 crore, which is an ROE of about minus 7.8%. Interest cover is 0.68x, far below the 2x covenant. Prakash is in technical default in the first bad quarter, not the second year.

What follows for Prakash:
1. Covenant breach gives lenders the right to recall or reprice. Any cross-default clause pulls in its other facilities.
2. It is now negotiating for waivers rather than running the business, and any new money comes at a higher spread or against more security, including possibly personal guarantees.
3. It cannot buy market share while competitors are weak, which is exactly when the best opportunities appear.

What follows for Nandan:
4. It can take a lower ROE for two years, keep investing, and buy distressed capacity or hire the people Prakash lets go.
5. Its 13.1% in good years looked unimpressive next to 21.6%. That gap was the price of the option it now gets to exercise.

The lesson: leverage is not just a return decision, it is a decision about who gets to act in a downturn. Compare the two companies over a full cycle, not in a single good year.

body.title: Leverage discipline for any company
steps: Calculate ROCE, not just profit growth, and compare it to your after-tax cost of debt
Ask what ROCE would be in your worst year of the past decade, not your average year
Check interest cover at that worst-year ROCE, not at current levels
Know your covenant thresholds and how far EBITDA can fall before you breach
Count operating leverage too: high fixed costs mean you should carry less debt
Keep refinancing dates spread out, so no single year carries a large repayment
When ROE is far above ROCE, be able to explain exactly how much of that gap is borrowed

cards.definition: Using borrowed money to amplify the return on the owners' capital, in both directions.
Operating profit as a percentage of all capital employed. It measures the business, not the funding.
Profit after tax as a percentage of shareholders' funds. It reflects both business and funding.
Borrowing helps shareholders only while ROCE exceeds the cost of debt.
When ROCE equals the cost of debt, leverage adds risk and nothing else.
Fixed operating costs magnifying the profit impact of revenue changes.
EBIT divided by interest. The first covenant to break when leverage is too high.
A rough indicator of how much of a company's return is borrowed rather than earned.

points: Leverage magnifies business performance. It does not improve it.
The test is a single comparison: return on capital employed against the cost of debt.
At ROCE of 20% and a 10% cost of debt, moving from no debt to D/E of 3 lifted ROE from about 15% to about 37% in our model.
At ROCE of 6%, the same leverage turned a 4.5% return into a 6% loss.
When ROCE equals the cost of debt, leverage adds risk and no return at all.
High operating leverage and high financial leverage compound each other, which is why volatile businesses should borrow less.
A high ROE sitting far above ROCE is borrowed, not earned. Check debt to equity before admiring it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Nandan Ceramics and Prakash Tiles are fictional. The nine-outcome model uses simplified assumptions, a single interest rate and a flat tax rate, and ignores depreciation, working capital movements and repayment schedules. Real leverage decisions require a full cash flow analysis.
